and assembled into spectral cubes using a customized notebook. Our notebook calls the standard JWST Science
Calibration Pipeline 1.9.6 (Bushouse et al. 2023), but includes custom steps focusing on background subtraction. The
key is that after source masking, the stage 1 rate files are median combined on a per detector/grating setting basis
to generate a master background. Due to time variable backgrounds, only sources observed within a month of each
other included in a particular master background. As demonstrated in Young et al. (in prep), our customized pipeline
achieves consistently better results than the standard pipeline alone with the achieved 1 σ RMS noise for each of the
12 MRS sub-bands essentially consistent with pre-flight expectations (Glasse et al. 2015). As a guideline the 1 σ RMS
noise is ≈1 −2 × 10−21W/m2 for the shorter wavelength sub-bands (corresponding to MRS channels 1 and 2), but is
more than an order of magnitude worse in the reddest sub-bands (corresponding to MRS channel 4).

Such a combination of ice absorption with superimposed CO gas absorption may in principle indicate the process of

It is unlikely that desorbing gas will have such a shift, hence this may argue in favor of an independent gas component.
If true, then redshifted absorption would be indicative of an inflow. Outflows are seen as blueshifted absorption or

we have in the center of the Milky Way for example (Sormani & Barnes 2019). Our galaxy also has the millimeter

4.3. Ice mantle composition analysis
Figure 8 shows how the derived column densities for CO2 vs. CO for FLS2 (z=0.494) compare with other sources in
the literature including our comparison heavily obscured Galactic objects (McClure et al. 2023) as well as YSOs (Noble
et al. 2013). We find a remarkably good correspondence such that while our source is on the whole less obscured the
relative numbers of CO2 vs. CO molecules in the line of sight are very similar to those comparison Galactic sources
with the CO2 molecule abundance in the ice mantles being ≈30% that of the CO molecules on average. We see a
very similar CO2 to CO ratio in the buried AGN spectrum of NGC4945. By contrast, while our other extragalactic
comparison spectra (NGC7469-ring and VV114-NE) both show clear CO2 absorption, neither have significant solid-
phase CO absorption.
As discussed in the Introduction ice mantle growth on dust grains is expected to proceed
through various stages with H20+CO2 mixture building up first, followed by CO freeze-out at higher densities which
can desorb back into the gas-phase as the temperature increases. The CO freeze-out is often accompanied by species
including the C≡N bond as in OCN−, as seen in our source as well as the comparison spectra of NGC4945 and W33 (see
Figure 7). Table 1 suggests the CO to OCN−, since we assumed the XCN feature is dominated by OCN−in deriving
the column density, ratio is roughly 5:1. Water ice is the dominant molecule; however, recall that its exact abundance
is uncertain due to the complex nature of the 6.0µm absorption feature as well as the uncertainty in de-blending it
from the PAH6.2 µm emission feature.
5. DISCUSSION
5.1. Evidence for a highly obscured nucleus in SSTXFLS J172458.3+591545
As discussed in the Introduction, ice mantle build-up requires high physical densities not just high dust column
densities. Our sources shows significant CO ice consistent with post CO freeze-out stage which is expected at n >
105 cm−3. This means that we need to have high density gas-dust clumps consistent with the presence of a compact
dusty nucleus (see discussion in
Spoon et al. 2004; Lai et al. 2020). The deep silicate feature alone is degenerate
between this model and one where the obscuring dust is extended galaxy-wide. Indeed, host galaxy obscuration is
observed in the correlations between silicate feature depth and galaxy inclination (Lacy et al. 2007a; Goulding et al.
2012). This helps explain the lack of correlation between the silicate depth and ice features depth, which is also seen
in the significantly variable ratios of the ice to silicate feature depths in Figure 3.
Our source’s ice absorption features are quite similar in shape to those seen in the spectrum of the NGC4945 nucleus
(see e.g. P´erez-Beaupuits et al. 2011), although the ones in our source are about 5 × less deep, as seen in Figures 7
and Figure 8. NGC4945 is a well studied very nearby, d ≈3.7 Mpc6 buried AGN. The high obscuration (AV ≈14)
in NGC4945 is due in part to it being observed through an edge-on disk. High resolution molecular gas and infrared

5.2. The relative strength of ice and silicate features
As discussed in the Introduction, the depth of the silicate features in galaxies does not correlate with the presence
or depth of ice features beyond the fact that ice features only appear in sources that show silicate absorption (at
least τsil ≈0.5). We can consider the silicate feature depth as proxy for the overall column of dust regardless of
whether it is distributed throughout the host galaxy or highly concentrated in clumps along the line of sight including
a compact, highly obscured nucleus as speculated above. However, clumpy AGN tori models struggle to reproduce the
deepest silicate absorption sources (e.g. Nenkova et al. 2000). Sources with τsil > 1 −2 require a more smooth dust
distribution either as a screen or a shell around a nucleus. They represent the distinct “buried nucleus” track in the
Spoon diagram with PAH equivalent width on one axis and the apparent silicate feature depth on the other (see e.g.
Spoon et al. 2007; Marshall et al. 2018; Sajina et al. 2022). On the other hand, as argued in Section 5.1, the stronger
the ice features, the higher the physical density which implies more compact structures along the line of sight.
We explore this model in Figure 9 which shows the CO2-to-silicate optical depth ratio vs. the silicate feature depth.

from Galactic sightlines. For the nearby buried AGN NGC4945, we extract the optical depth in CO2 from its Spitzer

This plot can be viewed roughly as increasing total dust column density along the x-axis and increasing compactness

This naive model is a reasonably good proxy for most of our comparison extragalactic spectra if we take AV ≈6.

5.3. The effect of beam dilution
The interpretation of Figure 9 has an important caveat that we already brought up in Section 5.1. Our spectrum
includes a large fraction of the galaxy – recall that the MIRI/MRS channel 1 PSF corresponds to a radius of 1.5kpc
for our source. This means that both the likely compact dusty nucleus as well as much of the host galaxy are included
in the beam. We model this beam dilution using Equation 2.
Fλ,model = bf × Fλ,nuclear + (1 −bf) × Fλ,host
(2)
Here Fλ,model models the observed spectrum around the ice feature (in this case the 4.27 µm CO2 feature), whereas
Fλ,nuclear and Fλ,host represent the separate spectra of the nucleus and host galaxy. The bf parameter represents the
fraction of the beam that’s filled with the emission from the dusty nucleus vs. the host galaxy. The higher spatial
resolution of our data, the larger the bf parameter and vice versa. In the limiting case of only nucleus included in
the spectrum, we have bf = 1 and the host galaxy contribution disappears. Conversely, as bf drops, the relative
contribution of the host increases, whereas that of the nucleus decreases.

the spatial resolution of the data because the optical emission of the AGN is much stronger than that of the host

6. SUMMARY & CONCLUSIONS
In this paper we study the ice absorption features in the JWST MIRI/MRS spectrum of FLS2, SSTXFLS
J172458.3+591545, a z = 0.494 source observed as part of the JWST GO1 program #1762 “Halfway to the Peak: A
Bridge Program To Map Coeval Star Formation and Supermassive Black Hole Growth” (see Young et al. 2025 in prep
for the full survey description). Here we summarize our findings:
• We detect the 4.27 µm 12CO2, the 4.62 µm XCN/OCN −, the 4.67 µm 12CO and the 6.0 µm water ice absorption
features. All ice feature profiles have analogs among known Galactic or extragalactic obscured sources.
• The relative strength of the CO2 and CO ice features is similar to that of much more highly obscured Galactic
sources with the CO2 column density being roughly 30% that of CO ice – suggesting similar patterns of ice
mantle growth across a wide range of obscuration.
• The presence of significant solid phase CO absorption with only hints of gas-phase CO is consistent with high
density (n > 105cm−3) and low temperatures of T ≈20 −90K.
• The above high densities imply the presence of a compact dusty nucleus as opposed to a model where all the dust
is distributed smoothly across the host galaxy. We estimate an AV ≈6 −7 for the optical extinction towards
this nucleus. Beam dilution effects mean this is a lower limit on the true nuclear optical depth.
• A plot of the observed τSi vs. τCO2/τSi is a rough proxy for the total dust column density on the x-axis vs. the
level of compactness of this dust on the y-axis. However, the limited beam covering fraction of the suggested
compact dusty nucleus means the measured ice features depth is a lower limit.
